title: Oramics
description: Four loops of clear 35mm film, lit from beneath on a black lightbox, run in step past one hard slit of light, the way Daphne Oram's machine read its stack of synchronised strips. Each strip holds one control: on the top one a drawn shape's height is the pitch and its weight how loud; the second is a mask on the volume, so a swelling ribbon swells and a gap gates; the third is the waveform itself, its density down the strip read as one cycle and turned into harmonics; the fourth sets the vibrato and how far into the room it goes. The loop arrives drawn by real hands, recorded pen and mouse traces from Quick, Draw!, and every mark is ink deposited by how long the brush dwelt: slow strokes pool and bead and dry to a darker rim, quick ones split into dry bristle streaks, and whatever you draw on any strip changes the sound the next time the loop comes round. Behind the light the reader prints what the machine plays onto a wide loop of its own below the four, a variable-area track slowed so every cycle shows: where the waveform strip changes from one broad band to a comb of lines, the printed cycle changes from a clear block to five growing teeth. The print comes off the head crisp and black; last lap's, still waiting upstream of the reader, has gone dull.
intent: Image is sound, after Daphne Oram's Oramics machine (https://www.daphneoram.org/?p=4469), where shapes drawn on strips of clear 35mm film set pitch and volume as they passed photocells, and Norman McLaren's Synchromy: what you see is what you hear.
